transcript:
Header: 2027-06-01 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~48min | Record: yes
Attendees: Sara Park (Redwood AE), Miguel Torres (Redwood SE), Hannah Lee (Redwood SE) -- Priya Nair (Aurora Head of ML), Ben Carter (Eng Manager), Liam O'Connor (SRE), Maya Singh (Product)

00:00 Sara: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros?
00:07 Priya: Hi, I'm Priya, head of ML at Aurora. We own the conversational fraud-detection assistant.
00:12 Ben: Ben here, engineering on infra and latency SLAs.
00:15 Liam: Liam, SRE, I'll handle network and VPC integration.
00:18 Sara: Awesome. Today's goal is a focused Optimize walkthrough: batching and prefix/K-V cache cost modeling, show how we reason about hit rates and token savings for your workload. Miguel will lead the demo.
00:30 Miguel: Cool, quick agenda: first talk about batching heuristics, then prefix vs k-v cache, then a cost model example using your numbers, and finish with pilot steps.
00:40 Maya: Sounds good, main success metric for us is under 150ms p50 and keeping token cost under $0.0009 per conversational turn on average.
00:52 Miguel: Great, we'll reference that.
01:05 Miguel: So batching, high level: we have continuous batching in the runtime that batches requests arriving within a short window. We tune the window to balance latency and throughput. For Aurora's 60k qps peak, we typically recommend a microbatch window of 10-25ms for latency-first workloads, or up to 100ms if you can accept higher p50 for better utilization.
01:30 Ben: Wait, 10-25ms windows — that seems tight. How do you guarantee not spiking p95?
01:37 Miguel: Good question. The runtime monitors queue depth and will adaptively shorten windows during tail spikes; also we support per-route SLOs so you can route strict-latency traffic to reserved pools or dedicated nodes.
01:52 Priya: For our assistant we have a lot of short prompts (10-40 tokens) plus a long context prefix (~1.2k tokens). How do caches help?
02:05 Miguel: This is exactly where prefix or K-V cache shines. Two patterns: prefix caching stores the token activations for repeated prefix sequences — e.g., static system prompts or recent conversation context. K-V cache is the model's attention KV cache for already computed past tokens; Redwood persists and reuses them across requests when safe.
02:25 Hannah: Practically, if your conversation keeps repeating a standard intro or system message, prefix cache can avoid recomputing the first ~400 tokens each request, saving compute. K-V cache helps with user-turn continuity to avoid recomputing the entire history.
02:40 Priya: Our typical flow: system prompt (700 tokens), doc chunk (200 tokens), and then user turn (20 tokens). So most work is the prefix.
02:49 Miguel: Exactly. We model hit rate based on canonicalization: if the system prompt is identical or normalized, hit rate can be 90%+ for prefix. If doc chunks vary but overlap, you can still get 30-50% effective reuse with smart chunking.
03:05 Ben: Show the numbers — what does that mean for cost?
03:10 Miguel: I'll pull up a quick cost calc with your numbers. (screen share) Baseline: average request generating 1500 total tokens (in+out), 700 are static prefix. If we can cache 70% of the prefix across requests, we avoid ~490 tokens of forward compute per request. At your volume that is ~490 * 100k requests/day = 49M tokens saved/day.
03:35 Miguel: Translating to cost, if compute cost is roughly $X per million tokens on our hosted model (we use an internal normalized $0.5 per 1M tokens as an example for this calc), that's ~ $24.5/day saved on token compute; but more meaningfully it reduces GPU utilization which can change instance sizing and reserved capacity needs, driving larger monthly savings.
04:00 Priya: The $0.5 per 1M seems off — our current vendor numbers are lower.
04:05 Sara: Right these numbers in the deck are placeholders; we'll run a pilot with your exact cost numbers. The point is the proportional savings from cache.
04:12 Miguel: Also remember there is a memory/throughput tradeoff: prefix cache requires memory to store activations per prefix key, and K-V cache requires more memory per session. We show a sample tradeoff table: more memory buys higher hit rate; beyond a point you hit diminishing returns.
04:30 Liam: For VPC/private deployments, how do we persist KV caches? Is that stored on local GPU or offloaded?
04:36 Miguel: In private/dedicated we keep KV in GPU memory for lowest latency; we can optionally spill to host memory or Redis-like store for long-tail sessions but that adds latency. For VPC we support customer-managed KMS and audit logs, and the cache persisted in customer VPC if you want full isolation.
04:55 Ben: On batching, do you expose the microbatch window or is it auto-managed?
05:00 Miguel: Both. We expose suggested configs in Redwood Optimize. You can set soft SLOs like target p50 and p95 and Optimize will recommend a batching window, max batch size, and whether to route to dedicated pools. We also provide a simulator to estimate cost/latency given traffic shape.
05:20 Miguel: Now the cost model — here's a simple spreadsheet: inputs: requests/day, avg tokens/request, prefix tokens, cache hit rate, tokens saved, compute cost per token. Outputs: estimated monthly dollars and percent reduction.
05:35 Priya: Can you share the spreadsheet after the call?
05:38 Miguel: Yes, we'll share the benchmark script and spreadsheet.
05:41 Miguel: Important caveat: caching correctness. For any PII or per-user secrets we need to ensure cache keys are scoped properly, TTLs, and privacy controls. For Aurora's regulated data we recommend per-tenant cache isolation and automatic redaction before caching.
06:00 Priya: That sounds right. We'll need SOC2 and encryption docs.
06:05 Sara: We'll include SOC2 Type II, ISO certs, and KMS integration notes in the security packet.
06:10 Liam: Network: if we do a private deployment we'll need egress IPs and allowlist; also any testing with dedicated GPUs will need port and CIDR info.
06:18 Sara: Noted — Liam will get that as an action item.
06:25 Miguel: Back to numbers: If we assume a 60% effective prefix hit rate and 30% KV reuse for the dynamic parts, combined token saving could be ~550 tokens/request which at your scale is material. Also batching reduces per-token kernel overhead — for small requests batching helps amortize fixed cost, for larger requests batching helps keep throughput high.
06:50 Ben: Any risks with caching freshness? Our docs update frequently, and we can't serve stale context.
06:55 Miguel: We support cache invalidation by key TTL and explicit invalidation APIs. You can also scope caches to session IDs so new doc updates automatically create new keys. We'll walk through TTL strategies in pilot.
07:12 Priya: For our SLAs, p95 must remain < 350ms. Will caching make p95 worse due to cache-miss spikes?
07:18 Miguel: Cache misses increase compute per request, but routing policies can route critical traffic to dedicated pools so p95 isn't impacted. Also adaptive batching and prefetch heuristics can warm caches for expected flows.
07:35 Miguel: Demo time — I'm going to run a small local sim with synthetic traffic shaped like Aurora's: 30% identical system prefix, 50% similar doc chunks, 20% unique. (typing/noise)
08:00 Miguel: Here you can see the simulator output: with a 25ms batch window and prefix cache 65% hit rate, p50 = 120ms, p95 = 280ms, tokens consumed/day down 41%, and estimated monthly compute 36% lower vs baseline.
08:25 Priya: Nice. What about memory footprint for that config?
08:28 Miguel: Roughly for your traffic we'd need ~120GB GPU memory reserved for KV/prefix caches across the cluster; that's an operational tradeoff to weigh against instance count reduction.
08:40 Ben: If we go Dedicated reserved capacity, how much flexibility do we have to change cache memory after commit?
08:45 Sara: You can adjust instance types and sizing on Dedicated but need to plan for capacity changes; we offer burst capacity and autoscaling policies to handle growth during pilot.
08:55 Miguel: One more piece: quantization and model selection. If you can quantize to 4-bit for less-critical paths, token compute cost drops and you might rely less on caching. Optimize will recommend quant+batching combos per route.
09:10 Priya: Could we run a split — core fraud-detection on higher precision/dedicated, and exploratory queries on quantized hosted?
09:16 Miguel: Yes, that's a common pattern. Redwood routing can do per-route model variants and fallbacks.
09:22 Maya: Questions from product: how do we audit what was cached? We need traceability for compliance.
09:28 Miguel: We have per-key audit logs and TTL/owner metadata; Optimize exposes cache hit metrics and traces per route in Console. We'll include sample screenshots in the packet.
09:40 Priya: Ok next steps I'm expecting: pilot with exact Aurora token pricing, run benchmarks on a sample dataset, and confirm VPC and KMS details.
09:50 Sara: We'll send pricing and contract, Miguel will share the benchmark script and perf spreadsheet. We can aim to start pilot next week pending contract.
09:58 Ben: Timeline sounds good.
10:05 Miguel: Quick common objections we often see: 1) "We can't trust caches with PII" — answer: per-tenant isolation and automatic redaction. 2) "Caching reduces freshness" — answer: TTLs and invalidation hooks. 3) "Memory costs offset savings" — answer: we model memory vs instance savings and often net positive.
10:40 Priya: Anything else on the pilot scope?
10:43 Sara: We'll include measurement plan: p50/p95 latency, tokens consumed, cache hit rate, monthly cost delta, and pass/fail thresholds aligned to your SLOs.
10:55 Miguel: I'll attach the simulation config we ran and the spreadsheet.
11:00 Sara: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the packet and schedule.
11:06 Priya: Thanks all.
11:10 End of recording
notes: Simulator outputs referenced: microbatch window 25ms -> p50 120ms p95 280ms; token savings ~41% in example; memory footprint ~120GB across cluster for cache. Security docs promised: SOC2, ISO, KMS integration. Benchmark artifacts: scripts, perf spreadsheet, simulation config.
